classification.difficultyReason: Adapt the supplied product proofs to the other laws, selecting reciprocal or common-root representations and justifying general rational-exponent identities without assuming the laws being proved.

inlines.text: Prove that the index laws hold for negative integer exponents. (Use the laws for positive integer exponents.)
For example, the product-of-powers result can be proved in the following way for negative integer exponents.

answer.short:
For non-zero bases, all five laws hold: $a^{-p}a^{-q}=a^{-(p+q)}$, $\dfrac{a^{-p}}{a^{-q}}=a^{q-p}$, $(a^{-p})^{-q}=a^{pq}$, $(ab)^{-p}=a^{-p}b^{-p}$ and $\left(\dfrac ab\right)^{-p}=\dfrac{a^{-p}}{b^{-p}}$.

Replace negative powers by reciprocals and use the positive-integer laws.
answer.worked:
Let $a,b\ne0$ and let $p,q$ be positive integers. Use $a^{-p}=\frac{1}{a^p}$.

Product:
$$\begin{aligned}a^{-p}a^{-q}&=\frac1{a^p}\frac1{a^q}\\a^{-p}a^{-q}&=\frac1{a^{p+q}}\\a^{-p}a^{-q}&=a^{-(p+q)}=a^{-p+(-q)}.\end{aligned}$$
Quotient:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a^{-p}}{a^{-q}}&=\frac{1/a^p}{1/a^q}\\\frac{a^{-p}}{a^{-q}}&=\frac{a^q}{a^p}\\\frac{a^{-p}}{a^{-q}}&=a^{q-p}=a^{-p-(-q)}.\end{aligned}$$
Here cancellation gives $a^{q-p}$ when $q\ge p$, and $\frac{1}{a^{p-q}}=a^{q-p}$ when $q<p$.

Power of a power:
$$\begin{aligned}(a^{-p})^{-q}&=\frac1{(a^{-p})^q}\\(a^{-p})^{-q}&=\frac1{(1/a^p)^q}\\(a^{-p})^{-q}&=a^{pq}=a^{(-p)(-q)}.\end{aligned}$$
Power of a product:
$$\begin{aligned}(ab)^{-p}&=\frac1{(ab)^p}\\(ab)^{-p}&=\frac1{a^pb^p}\\(ab)^{-p}&=a^{-p}b^{-p}.\end{aligned}$$
Power of a quotient:
$$\begin{aligned}\left(\frac ab\right)^{-p}&=\frac1{(a/b)^p}\\\left(\frac ab\right)^{-p}&=\frac{b^p}{a^p}\\\left(\frac ab\right)^{-p}&=\frac{a^{-p}}{b^{-p}}.\end{aligned}$$

inlines.text: Prove that the index laws hold for fractional exponents.
can be proved in the following way.
The result can easily be extended to

answer.short:
For $a,b>0$ and rational $r,s$, $a^ra^s=a^{r+s}$, $\dfrac{a^r}{a^s}=a^{r-s}$, $(a^r)^s=a^{rs}$, $(ab)^r=a^rb^r$ and $\left(\dfrac ab\right)^r=\dfrac{a^r}{b^r}$.

Write fractional powers as roots and use integer index laws; positive roots are unique.
answer.worked:
Let $a,b>0$, $r=\frac{p}{n}$ and $s=\frac{q}{m}$, where $p,q$ are integers and $n,m$ are positive integers. Put $c=\sqrt[nm]{a}$. Then $a^r=c^{pm}$ and $a^s=c^{qn}$ by the definition of rational powers.

Product:
$$\begin{aligned}a^ra^s&=c^{pm}c^{qn}\\a^ra^s&=c^{pm+qn}\\a^ra^s&=a^{(pm+qn)/(nm)}\\a^ra^s&=a^{r+s}.\end{aligned}$$
Quotient:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=\frac{c^{pm}}{c^{qn}}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=c^{pm-qn}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=a^{(pm-qn)/(nm)}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=a^{r-s}.\end{aligned}$$
Power of a power: let $d=\sqrt[n]{a}$ and $z=(a^{p/n})^{q/m}$. The definition of an $m$th root gives $z^m=(d^p)^q$; hence
$$\begin{aligned}z^{mn}&=((d^p)^q)^n\\z^{mn}&=d^{pqn}\\z^{mn}&=a^{pq}.\end{aligned}$$
Since $z>0$, uniqueness of the positive $mn$th root gives
$$\begin{aligned}(a^{p/n})^{q/m}&=a^{pq/(mn)}\\(a^r)^s&=a^{rs}.\end{aligned}$$
For the remaining laws put $u=\sqrt[n]{a}$ and $v=\sqrt[n]{b}$. Since $(uv)^n=ab$ and $(\frac{u}{v})^n=\frac{a}{b}$, uniqueness of positive roots gives $\sqrt[n]{ab}=uv$ and $\sqrt[n]{\frac{a}{b}}=\frac{u}{v}$.

Power of a product:
$$\begin{aligned}(ab)^{p/n}&=(uv)^p\\(ab)^{p/n}&=u^pv^p\\(ab)^{p/n}&=a^{p/n}b^{p/n}.\end{aligned}$$
Power of a quotient:
$$\begin{aligned}\left(\frac ab\right)^{p/n}&=\left(\frac uv\right)^p\\\left(\frac ab\right)^{p/n}&=\frac{u^p}{v^p}\\\left(\frac ab\right)^{p/n}&=\frac{a^{p/n}}{b^{p/n}}.\end{aligned}$$
The integer laws include negative numerators by part a, so these arguments also cover negative fractional exponents.
